findings.problem: The section opens the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) out-of-state oral Schedule III-V pathway and gives it a single timing figure - the practitioner's seven-day written follow-up - but never states the 30-day limit that decides whether such a prescription may be filled at all, nor the mandatory verification gate in the same subsection.
findings.rationale: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) provides that the paragraph 'shall be valid only for the purpose of authorizing the filling of prescriptions, issued within the preceding thirty days', and separately that 'if the substance is in schedules III to V, inclusive, the registered pharmacist shall verify the prescription by telephone or other means. A pharmacist shall not fill a prescription for which said verification cannot be obtained.' The section teaches, in timing_deadlines[0], that the Schedule III-IV window is six months from issue under 21 CFR 1306.22(a), and then in decision_logic[4] tells the pharmacist handling an out-of-state oral Schedule III-V prescription only to record that the written prescription was requested. A candidate applying the section to a 45-day-old out-of-state oral Schedule IV prescription would fill it on the six-month federal clock and would skip the required verification. Section 18(c) authorizes neither. This is the interaction defect pattern: the federal six-month period and the stricter Massachusetts 30-day gate sit in different fields and are never connected, and the state gate is the one that controls whether the fill is lawful. The repair is to state the 30-day issuance window and the verify-or-do-not-fill duty wherever the section invokes the s. 18(c) pathway.

findings.problem: The section tells the candidate that the federal one-time limit on a Schedule III-V refill transfer 'remains operative when the Massachusetts transfer rules are applied' and then, in the immediately following entry, that Massachusetts Schedule VI prescriptions 'transfer in the same manner as Schedule III-V prescriptions'. It never says that the federal one-time cap does not reach Massachusetts Schedule VI, and it never states the Massachusetts permission that governs instead.
findings.rationale: 247 CMR 9.14(4)(b) provides that 'Prescriptions for Schedule VI controlled substances may be transferred up to the maximum number of remaining refills authorized by the prescriber', and 9.14(4)(c) supplies the only ceiling - no transfer of a prescription authorizing refills more than one year from issuance. 21 CFR 1306.25 by its own terms governs only 'a controlled substance listed in Schedule III, IV, or V', that is, the federal schedules; a Massachusetts Schedule VI drug (105 CMR 700.002(F): all prescription drugs not in any other schedule) is not federally scheduled, so the federal one-time rule cannot cap its transfer. The section states 9.14(4)(c) accurately but omits 9.14(4)(b), and the adjacent placement of the two ma_vs_federal entries actively invites the wrong inference that a Schedule VI prescription, like a Schedule III-V one, may move only once. A candidate who has read learning objective 2 ('Recognize the special Massachusetts treatment of Schedule VI transfers') would refuse a lawful second Schedule VI transfer within the one-year window. Adding one clause - that Schedule VI transfers are capped by remaining prescriber-authorized refills and the one-year limit, not by the federal one-time rule - closes it.

findings.problem: The condition - 'A patient asks to move a controlled-substance prescription that has never been dispensed' - is broader than the pathway the action then prescribes. It omits the electronic, retail-pharmacy and state-law preconditions that make 21 CFR 1306.08(e) available.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.08(e) permits a one-time initial-dispensing transfer only of 'an electronic prescription for a controlled substance in Schedule II-V', only 'between retail pharmacies', and only 'upon request from the patient'; 1306.08(g) adds that it is 'permissible only if allowable under existing State or other applicable law', and 1306.08(f)(1)-(2) require the prescription to move in its electronic form, unaltered. A never-dispensed paper prescription has no federal transfer pathway at all: 21 CFR 1306.25 reaches only transfers 'for the purpose of refill dispensing'. The action text partly repairs the condition by saying 'keep the prescription electronic and unaltered', so a careful reader is unlikely to go wrong, but a candidate matching on the stated trigger would route a never-dispensed paper Schedule II prescription into a pathway that does not exist for it. Restricting the condition to an unfilled electronic prescription held at a retail pharmacy resolves it.

findings.problem: MA-Q-0009 is RELEASED but does not test the propositions this section teaches. It is a drug-classification and monitoring matrix item; four of its five options, including all four keyed-correct options, turn on material the section never states.
findings.rationale: MA-Q-0009 asks which pharmacy-system configurations are legally correct and keys A, B, C and D: pregabalin as Schedule V with MassPAT submission, gabapentin as federally noncontrolled but Massachusetts Schedule VI and PMP-reportable, methylphenidate as Schedule II with refills blocked, and CMEA retail controls on pseudoephedrine without reclassification. This section teaches Schedule III-V refill arithmetic and Massachusetts transfer mechanics; it contains no drug scheduling content (drug_examples is empty), no MassPAT reporting content and no CMEA content. Only distractor E - applying the federal Schedule III-IV five-refill/six-month rule to gabapentin because Massachusetts places it in Schedule VI - touches anything the section covers, and it does so through a Schedule VI inference the section never draws. Because the item is select-all-that-apply, a candidate who has studied only this section cannot answer it. The other two links are sound: MA-Q-0120 tests 247 CMR 9.14(4) and 247 CMR 8.04(4)(d) against quick_review[2], ma_vs_federal[1]-[2] and role_duties[3]; MA-Q-0397 tests 247 CMR 9.14(1)-(3) against quick_review[2] and decision_logic[3]. The repair is to relink this section to a refill- or transfer-testing item.

results.summary: Legally accurate on every provision I read against the controlling text, and unusually precise on the points that actually decide exam items - but it opens the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) out-of-state pathway without the 30-day gate that makes such a fill lawful, and it leaves the reach of the federal one-time transfer cap over Massachusetts Schedule VI unresolved. Confirmed sound: 21 CFR 1306.22(a) names only Schedules III and IV, imposes the six-month and five-refill limits independently, and 1306.22(e)(4) requires a new and separate prescription beyond either - matching quick_review[0], decision_logic[0] and timing_deadlines[0]. 247 CMR 9.04(13) reads 'may not fill or refill', and common_traps[7] catches exactly that, which a refill-only reading would miss; 9.04(15) does exclude institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 9.04(13), as exceptions[1] and decision_logic[2] say. 21 CFR 1306.25(a) states the one-time limit and the real-time online database alternative verbatim as quick_review[3] and exceptions[2] do, and 1306.25(b)(1)-(2) support role_duties[1]-[2] on pharmacist-to-pharmacist communication and the VOID annotation. 21 CFR 1306.08(e)-(g) confirm the separate initial-dispensing transfer, its Schedule II-V reach, its retail-pharmacy and patient-request conditions and the absence of any shared-database counterpart - quick_review[5] and exceptions[4] are right. 247 CMR 9.14(1)-(3) match quick_review[2] word for word, and 9.14(4)(c) really is limited to 'a prescription authorizing refills', which ma_vs_federal[1] and timing_deadlines[2] reproduce faithfully. 247 CMR 8.04(4)(d) confirms the certified technician's Schedule VI-only transfer authority with pharmacist-on-duty approval, against the federal two-pharmacist requirement - ma_vs_federal[2], role_duties[3] and common_traps[6] are correct. The hardest timing point in the section is also right: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) sets two days electronic and not more than seven days written under a s. 23(h) exception and excludes Schedule VI, while 105 CMR 721.070(B) sets seven BUSINESS days for oral Schedules II-V issued under a 721.070(A) exception; exceptions[3], timing_deadlines[4] and common_traps[4] flag the divergence rather than collapsing it into one number. exceptions[5] correctly tracks 105 CMR 721.070(C). Section 18(c) does place the seven-day clock on the practitioner's delivery or mailing while the pharmacist's duty is to record the request, so forms_records[0] and common_traps[2] read the statute correctly. Findings: the s. 18(c) 30-day issuance window and verification gate are absent (Medium); the Schedule VI transfer count under 247 CMR 9.14(4)(b) is never separated from the federal one-time cap (Medium); decision_logic[6]'s trigger is broader than 21 CFR 1306.08(e) (Low); and MA-Q-0009 tests classification, MassPAT and CMEA content this section does not teach (Low). All three linked questions are RELEASED. The defects are additive - text to insert, not text to correct - so MINOR_EDIT.

findings.problem: The section instructs the pharmacist not to reject a written Schedule VI prescription 'solely for that format' and describes the electronic-prescribing exception as removing 'that format mandate', but never names the Massachusetts form requirement that continues to govern the written prescription that the exception permits.
findings.rationale: 105 CMR 721.003 applies 105 CMR 721.000 to all prescriptions issued in the Commonwealth, and 721.020(A) requires every prescription to be electronic unless issued under a 721.070 exception. When 721.070(A)(9) lets a Schedule VI prescription be issued in writing, 721.020(F) governs it: a written prescription must bear the practitioner's signature and must be either transmitted by facsimile or similar technology or 'written on a tamper-resistant form consistent with federal requirements for Medicaid'. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(i) says the same at statute level. 105 CMR 721.040(A) then makes the consequence categorical: 'A Prescription in a format that does not conform to 105 CMR 721.000 is invalid and shall not be filled.' The section's forms_records field lists only the oral reduction to writing and the customer identifier. A candidate who follows decision_logic[1] would accept a written Schedule VI prescription on an ordinary non-tamper-resistant pad and dispense it; 721.040(A) forbids that fill. The gap is squarely inside scope, because the section's spine - learning objective 1, exceptions[0], common_traps[0] and role_duties[0] - is that the e-prescribing exception is narrow and other requirements survive it. Naming the tamper-resistant form and signature requirement among the surviving requirements is the repair.

findings.problem: The institutional sterile compounding pharmacy carve-out is stated as reaching only 247 CMR 9.04(12), although the same sentence also excludes 9.04(10) and 9.04(14) - both of which this section teaches elsewhere as unqualified duties.
findings.rationale: 247 CMR 9.04(15) reads: 'The requirements of 247 CMR 9.04(4), (5), (6), (9), (10), (12), (13), and (14) do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.' This section teaches 9.04(10) at exceptions[3] (count the day after the prescription was written as day one) and 9.04(14) at quick_review[4], forms_records[1] and decision_logic[4] (the customer identifier for a Schedule VI additional drug), each without qualification, and then presents the carve-out attached only to the validity rule in 9.04(12). A candidate reads that as a deliberate contrast and concludes that an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy still owes the customer-identifier and date-counting duties. It does not. Extending exceptions[2] to name 9.04(10) and 9.04(14) alongside 9.04(12) is a one-line fix.

findings.problem: The section's Schedule VI transfer treatment gives the pathway, the one-year ceiling and the certified-technician rule, but omits 247 CMR 9.14(4)(b), the provision that says how many times and how far a Schedule VI prescription may be transferred.
findings.rationale: 247 CMR 9.14(4)(b) provides that 'Prescriptions for Schedule VI controlled substances may be transferred up to the maximum number of remaining refills authorized by the prescriber.' decision_logic[2] routes the candidate through 9.14(4)(a)'s 'same manner as Schedules III-V' formula without stating 9.14(4)(b), so a candidate who carries over the familiar federal one-time-only rule for Schedules III-V (21 CFR 1306.25(a)) will cap a Schedule VI transfer at one. That rule does not apply: 1306.25 reaches only federally scheduled III, IV and V substances, and a Massachusetts Schedule VI drug is by definition not in any other schedule (105 CMR 700.002(F)). The linked question MA-Q-0120 keys the opposite proposition at choice B, so the omission also weakens the section against its own practice item. Adding 9.14(4)(b) to quick_review or decision_logic[2] closes it.

results.summary: Substantively the stronger of the two sections: every Massachusetts provision I read matched the section's statement of it, including several the guide states more precisely than its own rule summaries do. The one real defect is that the section tells a pharmacist to accept a written Schedule VI prescription without naming the form requirement that still makes it fillable. Confirmed sound: 105 CMR 700.002(F) defines Schedule VI as 'all prescription drugs, which are not included in any other schedule established by the Commissioner', supporting quick_review[0], ma_vs_federal[0] and common_traps[1]. 247 CMR 9.04(12) states the one-year validity, the bar on refilling after one year, and the professional-judgment continuation of a quantity not to exceed 14 days or the smallest available unit-of-use packaging - and it really does condition that continuation on both expiry-or-no-refills AND inability to obtain timely prescriber authorization, which exceptions[1] and decision_logic[3] reproduce conjunctively rather than loosening into an automatic emergency supply. 247 CMR 9.04(10) reads exactly as exceptions[3] says. 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9) is in fact 'Prescriptions issued for controlled substances in schedule VI', and 721.070(C) relieves the receiving pharmacist of verifying that an exception applies - quick_review[1] and role_duties[0] are right. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a) requires immediate reduction of an oral controlled-substance prescription to writing, and the closing sentence of s. 20(c) - 'The requirements of this subsection shall not apply to controlled substances in Schedule VI of section 3' - confirms that the carve-out reaches only the later follow-up prescription, exactly as quick_review[2] and exceptions[4] state. s. 22(a) supplies the required elements that survive, supporting exceptions[0]. On the additional-drug chain, 105 CMR 700.001 defines Additional Drug as a Schedule VI controlled substance determined to carry a bona fide potential for abuse, 700.012(C)(8) gives the Commissioner that determination and requires notice that dispensers 'must begin to report', and 247 CMR 9.04(14)(b) requires a customer identifier for Schedules II-V or an additional drug under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1), with 9.04(14)(c) making the hardship route conjunctive - documented reason AND printed name and address AND signature - which forms_records[1] states correctly. 247 CMR 8.04(4)(d) contains the word 'only' that common_traps[4] relies on. common_traps[2] is the sharpest item in the section and it is correct: 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) and 247 CMR 9.04(12) are two different one-year rules and neither restates the other. All three linked questions are RELEASED and on point - MA-Q-0116 on s. 20(a) versus the s. 20(c) carve-out, MA-Q-0118 on s. 22(a) elements surviving Schedule VI status, MA-Q-0120 on 247 CMR 9.14(4) and 8.04(4)(d). Findings: the surviving tamper-resistant written-form requirement is never named (Medium); the 247 CMR 9.04(15) carve-out is stated as reaching only 9.04(12) when it also reaches 9.04(10) and 9.04(14) (Low); and 247 CMR 9.14(4)(b) is omitted from the Schedule VI transfer treatment (Low). All three are insertions, so MINOR_EDIT.
